stimuli.text: A block of mass 2 kg on a 37° incline is connected by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass 7 kg. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.2. The system is released from rest, and the hanging block descends.
A block of mass 0.3 kg on a horizontal frictionless surface is attached to a spring. Its position is $$x(t) = 0.05\cos(5t)$$, with x in meters and t in seconds.
Students measure the period of a simple pendulum for several string lengths, using small amplitudes.
A solid cylinder (I = ½MR²) and a solid sphere (I = ⅖MR²) of equal mass M and radius R are released from rest at the top of the same ramp of height 0.8 m. Both roll without slipping.

questions.stem: A block slides down a 25° incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.2. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?

options.why: Friction acts up the slope.
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
Correct. a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ).
The component along the incline is mg sin θ.

questions.stem: A curve of radius 50 m is banked so that a car at 14 m/s needs no friction. What is the banking angle?

options.why: Square the speed.
Correct. tan θ = v²/(rg).
Use tan θ = v²/(rg), from dividing the force components.
Measure the angle from the horizontal.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal ledge 17 m high at 8 m/s. How far from the base of the ledge does it land?

options.why: Horizontal and vertical motion are independent.
Correct. Fall time from the height, times the horizontal speed.
Fall time is √(2h/g).
Take the square root for the time.

questions.stem: A motor lifts a 220 kg load 21 m at constant speed in 30 s. What average power does it deliver?

options.why: P = W/t.
That is the work; divide by time.
Include g.
Correct. P = mgh/t.

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 5x$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 1$$ m to $$x = 2$$ m?

options.why: The force is not constant.
Correct. W = ∫F dx.
Integrate; do not just evaluate F.
Divide by n + 1 when integrating.

questions.stem: A 0.4 kg ball hits a wall at 12 m/s and rebounds at 7 m/s. The contact lasts 0.07 s. What is the average force from the wall?

options.why: Divide by time.
Correct. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) with the direction reversed.
Include the rebound.
The velocity reverses, so the speeds add.

questions.stem: A system obeys $$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -49x$$. What is the period of its motion?

options.why: T = 2π/ω.
ω is the square root of the coefficient.
Correct. ω = √49 = 7 rad/s, T = 2π/ω.
T = 2π/ω, not 2πω.

questions.stem: A 1.8 kg mass oscillates on a spring with $$k = 80$$ N/m. What is the period?

options.why: That is the frequency.
The ratio is m/k.
Correct. T = 2π√(m/k).
Include the 2π.

questions.stem: A particle's position is $$x(t) = -3t^3 + 1t^2 - 1t$$, with x in meters and t in seconds. What is its acceleration at $$t = 3$$ s?

options.why: Bring each exponent down as a factor when differentiating.
Correct. Differentiate twice: a = 6at + 2b.
That is the velocity; differentiate again.
The derivative of 2bt is 2b, which also remains.

questions.explanation: a(t) = -18t + 2, so at t = 3 the value is -52.

questions.stem: A boat points straight across a river 100 m wide, moving at 5 m/s relative to the water. The current flows at 2 m/s. How long does the crossing take?

options.why: The current is perpendicular to the heading.
The current is perpendicular to the heading.
The perpendicular component alone sets the crossing time.
Correct. The current does not change the time to cross; it only carries the boat downstream.

questions.stem: A 4 kg cart moving at 8 m/s collides with and sticks to a 3 kg cart at rest. What is their speed after the collision?

options.why: Use m₁v₁ for the initial momentum.
Kinetic energy is not conserved here.
Correct. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.
The carts share the momentum.

questions.explanation: v_f = 4·8/7 = 4.57 m/s; kinetic energy lost = 54.9 J.

questions.stem: An oscillator's position is $$x(t) = 0.1\cos(4t)$$ m. What is its maximum acceleration?

options.why: Correct. a_max = Aω².
That is v_max.
Differentiate twice: Aω².
Multiply by the amplitude.

questions.stem: A 72 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is accelerating downward at 2 m/s². What does the scale read?

options.why: Correct. The scale reads the normal force: N − mg = ma (up positive).
The acceleration changes the normal force.
Check the direction of the acceleration.
Include gravity.

questions.stem: A ball is launched from level ground at 29 m/s at 70° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is its time of flight?

options.why: Correct. Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately.
That is the time to the top; the flight is twice as long.
Use v₀ sin θ.
Use the vertical component.

questions.explanation: v₀x = 9.92 m/s, v₀y = 27.3 m/s. T = 2v₀y/g = 5.56 s.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 1.1 m is pivoted at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration just after release?

options.why: Use τ = Iα with I = ML²/3.
τ = MgL/2.
The weight acts at L/2.
Correct. τ = Mg(L/2) and I = ML²/3 give α = 3g/(2L).

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 2x^2$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 2$$ m to $$x = 3$$ m?

options.why: Divide by n + 1 when integrating.
Correct. W = ∫F dx.
The force is not constant.
Integrate; do not just evaluate F.

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$7 \times 10^{23}$$ kg and radius $$1 \times 10^{6}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: Correct. ½mv² = GMm/R.
That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.
Potential energy uses 1/R.
Take the square root.

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 8 m down a 45° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.2. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Friction removes energy.
Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².
Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.

questions.stem: A wheel spinning at 19 rad/s slows uniformly to rest in 7 s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?

options.why: The average angular speed is ω₀/2.
Recheck the average.
That is in radians; convert to revolutions.
Correct. Δθ = ½ω₀t, then divide by 2π.

questions.stem: Two springs with constants 90 N/m and 60 N/m are connected in parallel and support a 1.5 kg mass at rest. How far do they stretch in total?

options.why: The force is the weight, mg.
Series and parallel rules are reversed.
Correct. k_eq = k₁ + k₂.
Both springs share the load.

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 90$$ N/m is compressed 0.21 m and launches a 0.1 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: Use energy: v = x√(k/m).
Take the square root.
Correct. ½kx² = ½mv².
The ½ appears on both sides.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 7 kg and radius 0.4 m spins at 13 rad/s on a frictionless axle. A 0.5 kg lump of clay is dropped onto the rim and sticks. What is the new angular speed?

options.why: Use rotational inertias, not masses.
Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.
Correct. Angular momentum is conserved: I_iω_i = I_fω_f.
The clay's inertia is mR².

questions.stem: A uniform 7 m beam weighing 200 N rests on supports at both ends. A 400 N load sits 5 m from the left end. What force does the right support exert?

options.why: The load is not at the center.
That is the left support's force.
Correct. Take torques about the left support.
Include the beam's weight at its center.

questions.stem: Masses of 4 kg and 1 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley. What is the tension in the string?

options.why: The lighter mass accelerates up, so T exceeds its weight.
The heavier mass accelerates down, so T is less than its weight.
Use T = m₂(g + a).
Correct. T = 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂).

questions.stem: A 1.5 kg ball on a 0.5 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the bottom of the circle its speed is 6 m/s. What is the tension in the string there?

options.why: Centripetal force uses v².
Include gravity.
Check the direction of gravity relative to the center.
Correct. At the bottom, T − mg = mv²/r.

questions.stem: A 2 kg mass hangs from a light string wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass 5 kg that turns on a frictionless axle. What is the acceleration of the mass?

options.why: For a disk, I/R² = M/2.
Correct. a = mg/(m + M/2), using I = ½MR² and a = Rα.
The pulley's inertia reduces the acceleration.
I/R² = M/2.

questions.explanation: mg − T = ma and TR = ½MR²(a/R) give a = 4.36 m/s².

questions.stem: A thin spherical shell rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 2.5 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: That is only correct for a hoop.
Some energy goes into rotation.
Rotational energy is ½Iω² = ½βmv².
Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ⅔MR².

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 4x^3 - 33x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.
Set the derivative, not U, to zero.
dU/dx = 3ax² − b.
Take the square root.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 12x² − 33 = 0 gives x = 1.66 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A 2 kg block on a horizontal table is connected by a string over a light pulley to a hanging 4 kg block. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the table and the block is 0.1. What is the acceleration of the blocks?

options.why: Both blocks accelerate; divide by the total mass.
Friction opposes the motion.
Include friction on the table block.
Correct. Net force (m₂g − μm₁g) divided by the total mass.

questions.stem: A rod lies along the x-axis from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 4$$ m and has linear mass density $$\lambda = kx^3$$. Where is its center of mass?

options.why: Integrate x·xⁿ and xⁿ correctly.
The exponents are n + 2 and n + 1.
Correct. x_cm = ∫xλ dx / ∫λ dx.
The rod is not uniform.

questions.stem: A constant torque of 8 N·m acts on a wheel ($$I = 0.8$$ kg·m²) initially at rest, through 2 revolutions. What is the wheel's final angular speed?

options.why: Convert revolutions to radians.
W = ½Iω².
½Iω² = W; solve for ω.
Correct. Work τΔθ (in radians) equals ½Iω².

questions.stem: A 500 kg car heading east at 20 m/s collides with a 2000 kg car heading north at 9 m/s, and they lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?

options.why: Weight each velocity by its mass.
Correct. Conserve momentum in x and y separately, then combine.
Momentum is a vector; add components at right angles.
Divide by the total mass.

questions.stem: An object of mass 0.9 kg falls from rest with a drag force $$F = -bv$$, where $$b = 0.2$$ kg/s. What is its speed at $$t = m/b$$?

options.why: The approach is exponential.
Terminal speed is reached only as t → ∞.
Correct. v = v_T(1 − e^(−t/τ)) and t = τ.

questions.explanation: v_T = mg/b = 44.1 m/s and τ = m/b = 4.5 s.

questions.stem: A 4 kg ball moving at +4 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 7 kg ball at rest. What is the velocity of the 7 kg ball afterward (positive in the original direction)?

options.why: Correct. Elastic: conserve momentum and kinetic energy (relative velocity reverses).
That would be a sticking collision.
Only equal masses exchange velocities.
Kinetic energy is conserved too.

questions.explanation: v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v/(m₁ + m₂) = -1.09 m/s; v₂' = 2m₁v/(m₁ + m₂) = 2.91 m/s.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 2 kg and radius 0.6 m rotates about an axis perpendicular to it, 1.5 m from its center. What is its rotational inertia?

options.why: The axis is not through the center.
Include the disk's own I about its center.
Correct. Parallel-axis theorem: I = ½MR² + Md².
The parallel-axis term is Md².

questions.stem: Satellite B orbits a planet in a circular orbit 9 times the radius of satellite A's circular orbit. What is the ratio of B's orbital period to A's?

options.why: The exponent is 3/2.
T² ∝ r³.
Correct. T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2).
Kepler's third law: T ∝ r^(3/2).

questions.stem: A mass on a spring oscillates with angular frequency 7 rad/s and amplitude 0.07 m. What is its speed when it is 0.014 m from equilibrium?

options.why: Use A² − x² under a square root.
Speed is greatest at equilibrium, not at the ends.
That is the maximum speed, at x = 0.
Correct. v = ω√(A² − x²), from conservation of energy.

questions.stem: An object's acceleration is $$a(t) = 2t$$ m/s². At $$t = 0$$ it has velocity 6 m/s and is at $$x = 0$$. What is its velocity at $$t = 4$$ s?

options.why: Correct. Integrate a(t) and add the initial velocity.
Integrating tⁿ divides by n + 1.
The acceleration is not constant, so constant-acceleration equations do not apply.
Include the initial velocity.

questions.stem: A 3 kg object at rest experiences a net force $$F(t) = 11t$$ N from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 4$$ s. What is its final speed?

options.why: Divide by the mass to get speed.
Correct. Impulse ∫F dt equals the change in momentum.
The force is not constant.
Integrate the force over time.

questions.explanation: J = ∫F dt = 88 N·s; v = J/m = 29.3 m/s.

questions.stem: A 24 g bullet moving at 450 m/s embeds in a 4 kg block hanging from strings. How high does the block rise?

options.why: Correct. Momentum for the collision, then energy for the swing.
Kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision.
h = V²/(2g).
Find the block's speed after the collision first.

questions.explanation: V = 2.68 m/s after the collision; h = V²/(2g) = 0.368 m.

questions.title: Block on an incline with a hanging mass

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a free-body diagram for the 2 kg block, labeling each force.

rubric.criterion: Weight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline, tension up the incline.
Kinetic friction down the incline (opposite the motion).

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the acceleration of the system in terms of the masses, θ, μ and g, then calculate its value.

rubric.criterion: Newton's second law applied to each block (or the system).

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string.
Calculate the speed of the blocks after the hanging block has descended 0.5 m, and the work done by friction on the incline block during that motion.

rubric.criterion: Work by friction, with a negative sign.

parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) graphs of position, velocity and acceleration versus time for one period, aligned vertically.

rubric.criterion: Position is a cosine starting at +A; velocity is a negative sine starting at 0.
rubric.example: x starts at 0.05 m; v starts at 0 and goes negative.

rubric.criterion: Acceleration starts at its negative maximum and is opposite in sign to position throughout.

parts.prompt: Derive expressions for v(t) and a(t), and determine the maximum speed and maximum acceleration.
Calculate the spring constant and the period.
Calculate the total mechanical energy and describe how kinetic and potential energy vary during one period.

rubric.example: K is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A; U is the reverse; the sum is constant. Each varies twice per period.

parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to measure the period accurately, including how to reduce uncertainty.

rubric.example: Time 10 swings with a stopwatch and divide by 10.

rubric.criterion: Keep the amplitude small and repeat trials.
rubric.example: Release from under about 10° and average several trials.

parts.prompt: Identify quantities to graph that would give a straight line, and explain how g can be found from the graph.
Plot (describe) the linearized data and draw a best-fit line. Use it to calculate an experimental value of g.
The students repeat the experiment with a much larger amplitude. Predict how the measured periods would change and explain.

rubric.criterion: Periods increase slightly; the small-angle approximation (sin θ ≈ θ) no longer holds.
rubric.example: The restoring torque is less than proportional to θ at large angles.

parts.prompt: Without calculating, predict which object reaches the bottom first. Justify your prediction using energy.

rubric.example: It has the smaller rotational inertia per MR².

rubric.criterion: Justification: less of its energy goes into rotation, so more is translational kinetic energy.

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed at the bottom of an object with rotational inertia βMR², in terms of g, h and β.

rubric.criterion: Energy conservation including both forms of kinetic energy, with v = Rω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of each object at the bottom.

rubric.example: solid cylinder: 3.23 m/s; solid sphere: 3.35 m/s

parts.prompt: Explain whether your derived expression is consistent with your prediction in part (a), and why neither speed depends on M or R.

rubric.criterion: Smaller β gives larger v, consistent with the prediction.
M and R cancel in the energy equation.
rubric.example: Only the shape factor β matters.
